lessons.unit: Summer 1: Rivers and the water cycle (Flow and One Planet, Our World)
lessons.title: The water cycle
lessons.bigQuestion: Could the water in your glass today once have been part of a cloud over the sea?
objectives: To understand how water moves around the Earth in the water cycle
successCriteria: All: name the four stages of the water cycle
Most: explain evaporation and condensation
Some: use the water cycle to explain where rain comes from
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: states of matter (liquid and gas)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how rain is sent down in measure

keywords.def: water heated by the Sun turns into water vapour
water as an invisible gas in the air
water vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops
water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail
water gathering in seas, rivers, lakes and the ground

hook.text: Puddles disappear on a sunny day. Where does the water go?

islamicLink.text: Allah says He sends down water from the sky in due measure and settles it in the earth (Al-Mu'minun 23:18). The water cycle is part of how He provides for every living thing.

starter.q: Name one thing the Iron Age Britons built.
starter.a: For example: hill forts or roundhouses

teach.heading: Water keeps moving
bullets: The same water is used again and again
It moves between sea, sky and land
teach.note: There is no new water: it goes round and round.

teach.heading: Up into the sky
bullets: The Sun heats seas and lakes
teach.note: Breath on a cold window makes condensation: the same idea.

teach.heading: Back down to Earth
bullets: Drops in clouds join and grow heavy
Water collects in rivers, lakes and seas
teach.note: Rivers carry the water back to the sea, and the cycle starts again.

teach.heading: Water cycle in a bowl
bullets: Cling film on top, ice on the film
teach.note: Model the home demo. An adult pours the warm (not boiling) water.

model.problem: Make a water cycle in a bowl
steps: Adult pours warm water into a bowl
Wait 10 minutes and look under the film
model.answer: Drops condense under the cold film and drip back down

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Water vapour turning back into drops is:
check.why: Condensation is cooling vapour into drops; evaporation is the opposite.

practice.q: What turns water into water vapour?
practice.model:
The Sun shines on the sea.
The water gets warm.
It turns into vapour and rises.
This is evaporation.

practice.q: Name two kinds of precipitation.
Where does river water go?

independent.q: Core: Draw and label the water cycle diagram: sea, Sun, clouds, rain, mountain, river, with the four stages and arrows.
independent.a: A labelled cycle with evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection in the right places
independent.model: Teacher draws the sea and the first arrow for evaporation.

independent.q: Extend: Write what happened in the bowl demo using two key words.
independent.a: Warm water evaporated; the vapour condensed on the cold film and dripped back down

independent.q: Stretch: Why does it rain more over mountains?
independent.a: Air rises over mountains and cools, so vapour condenses and rain falls

exit.q: Clouds form by:
exit.a: Condensation

exit.q: Big question: could your water have been in a cloud?
exit.a: Yes: the same water goes round the cycle from sea to cloud to rain to river

lessons.homework: Try the water cycle in a bowl (or a sealed bag of water taped to a sunny window) and draw what you see after one hour.
lessons.send: SEND: diagram with labels to cut and stick. EAL: four stage words with pictures. Stretch: add groundwater and plants to the diagram.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 3 curriculum map and history and geography long-term plans 2023-24; TGA Year 3 pack, History and geography, Summer 1 Flow (+ One Planet, Our World) (Cornerstones Maestro Flow and Emperors and Empires: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Water cycle diagram sheet (portal printable)
Household items: bowl, warm water (adult pours), cling film, ice cubes

pictures.alt: A diagram of the water cycle

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Rivers and the water cycle (Flow and One Planet, Our World)
lessons.title: A river's journey from source to mouth
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a river always flow downhill to the sea and never back up?
objectives: To understand how a river changes on its journey from source to mouth
successCriteria: All: label source, tributary, meander and mouth
Most: describe how a river changes downstream
Some: explain why rivers make meanders
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: rivers as a sign of Allah's mercy, bringing water to land

keywords.def: where a river begins
a smaller river that joins a bigger one
a big bend in a river
where a river meets the sea
the wide end of a river where it meets the tide

hook.text: If you dropped a leaf in a stream on a hill, where might it end up?

islamicLink.text: Allah tells us He made from water every living thing (Al-Anbiya 21:30). Rivers carry this water across the land to people, animals and plants.

starter.q: Water vapour cools to make clouds by:
Name the four stages of the water cycle.

teach.heading: Where rivers start
bullets: Rain falls on hills and mountains
A spring or stream is the source
teach.note: Link to the water cycle: rivers are the collection stage.

teach.heading: Growing bigger
bullets: The river gets wider and deeper
teach.note: Where two rivers meet is a confluence (extra word for the keen).

teach.heading: Bends and the sea
bullets: Lower down the river is slow and wide
It ends at the mouth or estuary
teach.note: Show an aerial photo of a meander.

teach.heading: Label a river
bullets: Source at the top of the hill
teach.note: Model labelling the river diagram.

steps: Find a small river joining: tributary

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: A smaller river that joins a bigger one is a:
check.why: A tributary joins the main river; a meander is a bend; the mouth is the end.

practice.q: Where does a river begin?
practice.model:
I follow the river uphill.
It gets smaller and smaller.
Where it starts is the source.

practice.q: Is a river faster near the source or the mouth?
What is a big bend in a river called?

independent.q: Core: Label the river diagram with source, tributary, meander, estuary and mouth, and add arrows to show the flow.
independent.a: All five labels correct; arrows flow from source to mouth
independent.model: Teacher labels the source first and draws the first arrow.

independent.q: Extend: Write three sentences describing the river from source to mouth.
independent.a: For example: It starts as a small fast stream in the hills. Tributaries join it. It meanders slowly to the sea.

independent.q: Stretch: Why does a river always flow downhill?
independent.a: Gravity pulls the water down towards lower land and the sea

exit.q: Where a river meets the sea is the:
exit.a: Mouth

exit.q: Big question: why does a river flow downhill?
exit.a: Gravity pulls water from high land down to the sea

lessons.homework: Find a river near you on an online map with an adult. Follow it: where is its mouth?
lessons.send: SEND: labels to cut and stick. EAL: river words with pictures. Stretch: find a river with an estuary in the UK.

River journey diagram (portal printable)
Online map with an adult

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Rivers and the water cycle (Flow and One Planet, Our World)
lessons.title: UK counties and cities: London and the River Thames
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one river flow past fields, villages and a capital city on the same journey?
objectives: To understand how the UK is divided into counties and cities, using the River Thames as an example
successCriteria: All: name some counties the Thames flows through
Most: find cities on the Thames
Some: explain how the Thames Barrier protects London
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Londinium was built on the Thames
lessons.smsc: Social: protecting a city where millions of people live

keywords.def: an area of a country with its own name and council
a large, important town
the river that flows through London to the North Sea
water covering land that is usually dry
giant gates that protect London from floods

hook.text: If you could follow the Thames from its source, what would you see first and last?

starter.q: Name one of the four countries of the UK.
starter.a: England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland

teach.heading: Counties
bullets: Each has towns, villages and countryside
teach.note: Show a county map of England.

teach.heading: The Thames' journey
bullets: Through London to the North Sea
teach.note: About 346 km long. Follow it on the map with your finger.

timeline.label: Mouth
timeline.text: The Thames Estuary and North Sea

teach.heading: London and the river
bullets: Romans built Londinium by the Thames
Ships brought goods to its docks
teach.note: Link to history: a river crossing made London a good place for a city.

teach.heading: Keeping London safe
bullets: The Thames Barrier closes its gates
teach.note: Model how the barrier works.

model.problem: How does the barrier stop a flood?
steps: A very high tide comes up from the sea
The gates rise up from the river bed
The sea water is held back

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: The Thames reaches the sea in the east, at the Thames Estuary on the North Sea.

practice.q: Which county is the Thames' source in?
practice.model:
I go to the start of the river on the map.
It is in the west.
The county there is Gloucestershire.

practice.q: Name a city on the Thames apart from London.
What protects London from high tides?

independent.q: Core: On the map, follow the Thames and label: its source, Oxford, Reading, London, the Thames Barrier, the estuary, and two counties.
independent.a: Correct labels in order from west to east
independent.model: Teacher labels the source in Gloucestershire first.

independent.q: Extend: Name your own county or the nearest city to you.
independent.a: The pupil's county or city

independent.q: Stretch: Why might the Thames Barrier be needed more in the future?
independent.a: Sea levels are rising, so high tides may get higher

exit.q: Oxford is a:
exit.a: City on the Thames

exit.q: Big question: what does the Thames pass on its journey?
exit.a: Countryside and villages, then towns like Reading and cities like Oxford and London, then the sea

lessons.homework: Find your county on a map with an adult and list three towns or cities in it.
lessons.send: SEND: map with places numbered to label. EAL: county, city, river, flood with pictures. Stretch: find two tributaries of the Thames.

Map of the River Thames and southern England counties (portal printable)
Atlas or online map

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Rivers and the water cycle (Flow and One Planet, Our World)
lessons.title: One planet: how people use and share water
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it fair that some people have more water than they need while others have too little?
objectives: To understand how people around the world use water and why it must be shared and saved
successCriteria: All: name the seven continents and five oceans
Most: record how my home uses water in a day
Some: suggest ways to share and save water
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: tally charts and bar charts
lessons.smsc: Moral: sharing a gift fairly and not wasting it

keywords.def: one of seven very large areas of land
one of five huge areas of salt water
a long time with too little rain
use carefully so it lasts
people who live and share things together

hook.text: How many times do you think your family turns on a tap in one day?

islamicLink.text: Allah tells us to eat and drink but not to waste (Al-A'raf 7:31). The Prophet ﷺ made wudu with very little water (Bukhari and Muslim), even when water was plentiful. Saving water is part of thanking Allah.

starter.q: Name the four stages of the water cycle.

teach.heading: Seven continents, five oceans
teach.note: Show the world map. Most of Earth's water is salty sea water.

teach.heading: How we use water
bullets: Farms and factories use the most
teach.note: In the UK each person uses about 140 litres a day at home.

teach.heading: Not everywhere has enough
bullets: Some walk far to fetch water
teach.note: Water is shared by communities and countries along a river.

teach.heading: Home fieldwork: a water tally
bullets: Tally every tap, flush and wash
teach.note: Model a tally for the morning.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: A long time with too little rain is a:
check.why: A drought means too little rain; a flood means too much water.

practice.q: Which ocean is the largest?
practice.model:
I look at the world map.
The ocean between Asia and America is huge.
It is the Pacific.

practice.q: Name two ways your family uses water.
Name one way to save water.
practice.a: Turn off the tap while brushing teeth, shorter showers, fix drips

independent.q: Core: Use your water tally (from home or the sample tally sheet) to make a bar chart of how your family uses water.
independent.a: A bar chart with labelled uses and correct bar heights
independent.model: Teacher draws the first bar from the model tally.

independent.q: Extend: Write three ways your family could conserve water.
independent.a: For example: fill a cup for teeth, a full washing machine only, a bowl for washing fruit

independent.q: Stretch: Why might countries sharing one river disagree?
independent.a: If one country takes more water upstream, less reaches people downstream

exit.q: There are how many continents?
exit.a: Seven

exit.q: Big question: is it fair? What should we do?
exit.a: No; we should use water carefully and share it, as Islam teaches

lessons.homework: Keep the water tally for a whole day with your family and bring the totals for the end-of-unit quiz.
lessons.send: SEND: tally sheet with pictures. EAL: continent and ocean names with a map. Stretch: compare UK water use with a country in drought.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 3 curriculum map and history and geography long-term plans 2023-24; TGA Year 3 pack, History and geography, Summer 1 Flow (+ One Planet, Our World) (Cornerstones Maestro Flow and Emperors and Empires: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Home water-use tally sheet with a sample tally (portal printable)
Squared paper for the bar chart
Flow end-of-unit quiz and labelled river diagram (portal quiz; assessed)

pictures.alt: A map of the continents and oceans

lessons.title: Where are the rainforests?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do rainforests grow near the Equator and not in Britain?
objectives: To understand where the world's tropical rainforests are and why they grow there
successCriteria: All: find the Equator and the tropics on a world map
Most: locate the Amazon and Congo rainforests and their continents
Some: explain why rainforests grow between the tropics
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: plants need water, light and warmth
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at the variety of Allah's creation

keywords.def: a thick forest with a lot of rain all year
an imaginary line round the middle of the Earth
the hot area between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
one of seven very large areas of land
the largest rainforest, in South America

hook.text: Which is easier to grow a jungle in: a hot wet place or a cold dry place? Why?

islamicLink.text: Allah sends the rain and brings plants out of the earth. Allah says He sends down water from the sky and with it brings out gardens full of beauty (an-Naml 27:60). The rainforests near the Equator show how much life Allah brings from rain.

starter.q: Which ocean is between Europe and North America?
Name the continent we live on.

teach.heading: Lines on the globe
bullets: The Equator goes round the middle
Tropic of Cancer is north of it
Tropic of Capricorn is south of it
teach.note: Show a globe or world map. Trace the Equator, then the two tropics. The area between is the tropics.

teach.heading: The world's rainforests
teach.note: Point to each on the map. All are near the Equator.

teach.heading: Why there?
bullets: The Sun is high all year: hot
Warm air rises and makes rain
Hot plus wet: plants grow fast
teach.note: Explain simply: near the Equator it is hot every day and it rains most days, so plants grow all year.

teach.heading: The Amazon
bullets: The River Amazon flows through it
teach.note: The Amazon covers parts of nine countries; most of it is in Brazil.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share.

check.q: Which line do most rainforests lie close to?
check.why: Rainforests are in the hot, wet tropics near the Equator. The Arctic Circle is cold; the Prime Meridian runs north to south.

practice.q: Which continent is the Amazon rainforest in?
practice.model:
Find the Amazon on the map.
Look at the land around it.
It is in South America, mostly in Brazil.

practice.q: Which continent is the Congo rainforest in?
Is the UK in the tropics?
practice.a: No, it is far north of the Tropic of Cancer

independent.q: Core: On a blank world map, draw the Equator and the two tropics, then shade the Amazon and Congo rainforests.
independent.a: Equator across the middle, tropics either side; Amazon in northern South America, Congo in central Africa
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: a red line for the Equator through Brazil and Congo, dotted lines for the tropics, green shading for the rainforests.

independent.q: Extend: Label the continents your rainforests are on.
independent.a: South America and Africa (and Asia if Borneo is added)

independent.q: Stretch: Write one sentence: Rainforests grow near the Equator because ...
independent.a: ... it is hot and wet all year, so plants can grow all the time

exit.q: The Amazon is in:
exit.a: South America

exit.q: Big question: why do rainforests grow near the Equator and not in Britain?
exit.a: Near the Equator it is hot and rains a lot all year; Britain is too cold in winter and not wet enough all year

lessons.homework: Find three foods in your kitchen that may come from tropical countries and look up where they grow.
lessons.send: SEND: a map with the Equator already drawn and dots to shade. EAL: Equator, tropics, rainforest with pictures. Stretch: add the rainforests of South-East Asia.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 3 curriculum map and history and geography long-term plans 2023-24 (Mighty Metals); TGA Year 3 pack, History and geography, Spring 1 (Cornerstones Maestro: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Blank world map with the Equator and tropics (portal printable)
Atlas or online world map shared on screen
Green, red and blue pencils
Mini-whiteboard and pen

The River Amazon winding through the forest

lessons.title: The layers of the rainforest
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does each layer of the rainforest feel like a different world?
objectives: To understand how the rainforest is made of layers with different light and life
successCriteria: All: name the four layers in order
Most: describe the light and plants in each layer
Some: explain why the forest floor is dark
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah's care for every creature

keywords.def: the tallest trees that stick out above the rest
the thick roof of leaves
the dim layer of small trees and bushes
the dark ground at the bottom
one level on top of another

hook.text: If you climbed from the ground to the top of a rainforest tree, what would change as you went up?

islamicLink.text: Allah made every living thing in pairs and in its place. In the rainforest each layer has its own plants and animals, all looked after by Allah. Allah says there is no creature on earth except that Allah provides for it (Hud 11:6).

starter.q: Name the imaginary line round the middle of the Earth.

teach.heading: Four layers
teach.note: Draw four stacked boxes. Say them together from top to bottom.

teach.heading: Emergent and canopy
bullets: Emergent trees can grow over 50 m
teach.note: The canopy is like an umbrella. It catches most of the sunlight.

teach.heading: Understorey and forest floor
bullets: Plants have big leaves to catch light
teach.note: Ask: why might plants down here have huge leaves? To catch the little light there is.

teach.heading: Light in each layer
teach.note: Only a tiny part of the sunlight reaches the forest floor; use the chart as a picture of 'a lot' to 'very little'.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which layer is the 'roof' of the rainforest?
check.why: The canopy is the thick roof of leaves. The understorey is below it and the forest floor is at the bottom.

practice.q: Put the layers in order from the top.
practice.model:
Start at the very top: emergent.
Then the roof of leaves: canopy.
Then the dim middle: understorey.
Last, the ground: forest floor.

practice.q: Which layer is darkest?
Where do most rainforest animals live?

independent.q: Core: Draw and label the four layers. Add one fact about each.
independent.a: Four labelled layers with facts such as: emergent, tallest trees; canopy, most animals; understorey, dim; forest floor, dark and leafy
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: draw the tall emergent tree, write 'emergent: tallest trees, over 50 m'.

independent.q: Extend: Add an arrow showing where the light comes from and how it gets less.
independent.a: An arrow from the top getting thinner towards the floor

independent.q: Stretch: Why do fallen leaves rot quickly on the forest floor?
independent.a: It is hot and wet, so tiny living things break them down fast

exit.q: The emergent layer is:
exit.a: The tallest trees

exit.q: Big question: why does each layer of the rainforest feel like a different world?
exit.a: Each layer gets a different amount of light, so different plants and animals live there

lessons.homework: Make a rainforest layers fold-out from a strip of paper folded into four.
lessons.send: SEND: layer labels to stick in the right boxes. EAL: top, middle, bottom, light, dark. Stretch: research one animal for each layer.

Rainforest layers diagram sheet (portal printable)
Atlas or online world map shared on screen
Coloured pencils
Mini-whiteboard and pen

pictures.alt: An emergent tree above the canopy

lessons.title: Rainforest climate and weather
lessons.bigQuestion: What would a week of weather be like in the Amazon?
objectives: To understand how the rainforest climate is hot, wet and humid all year
successCriteria: All: say that the rainforest is hot and wet
Most: read the rainfall for a month from a bar chart
Some: compare the rainforest climate with London's
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: rain as a sign of Allah

keywords.def: the usual weather of a place over many years
what it is like outside today
the air feels damp and sticky
how much rain falls
how hot or cold it is

hook.text: Would you rather live where it rains a little every day, or a lot in some months and hardly at all in others?

islamicLink.text: Allah drives the clouds and sends the rain. Allah says He sends the winds which stir up clouds, spreads them in the sky as He wills, and rain comes out of them (ar-Rum 30:48). The daily storms of the rainforest are this sign at work.

starter.q: What is the line round the middle of the Earth called?

teach.heading: Weather and climate
teach.note: Ask: is 'it is raining now' weather or climate? Weather.

teach.heading: Hot all year
bullets: The Sun is high near the Equator
teach.note: Manaus, a city in the middle of the Amazon, is about 27 °C in most months.

teach.heading: Wet all year
bullets: Over 2,000 mm of rain a year
teach.note: Rough monthly rain for Manaus (rounded). It is still wet in the 'dry' season compared with many places.

teach.heading: Humid
bullets: The air is full of water
teach.note: Trees give out water from their leaves, which rises and helps make more rain.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: The usual weather over many years
check.why: Climate is the usual pattern over many years; weather is what happens today.

practice.q: From the chart, how much rain falls in Manaus in March?
practice.model:
Find March on the bottom.
Go up to the top of the bar.
Read across: about 330 mm.

practice.q: Which month on the chart is driest?
London gets about 50 mm in a month. Is Manaus wetter or drier in March?

independent.q: Core: Write a weather report for a day in the Amazon. Use: hot, humid, rain, storm.
independent.a: For example: It is 27 °C and humid. In the afternoon there is a heavy storm.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Good morning from Manaus. It is already 26 °C and the air feels sticky. Heavy rain will fall this afternoon.'

independent.q: Extend: Give two differences between the Amazon climate and London's.
independent.a: The Amazon is hotter all year and much wetter; London has a cold winter

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why it rains so much in the rainforest.
independent.a: The hot sun makes warm wet air rise, it cools, makes clouds and heavy rain

exit.q: The rainforest climate is:
exit.a: Hot and wet all year

exit.q: Big question: what would a week of weather be like in the Amazon?
exit.a: Hot (about 27 °C), humid, with heavy rain or storms most days

lessons.homework: Keep a five-day weather diary at home and compare it with the Amazon.
lessons.send: SEND: a word mat for the report and a picture of a storm. EAL: hot, wet, humid, storm with pictures. Stretch: plot London's rainfall on the same chart.

Weather report writing frame (portal printable)
Manaus rainfall chart (on the slide; portal printable)
Mini-whiteboard and pen

pictures.alt: A heavy rain storm over a tropical forest

lessons.title: Rainforest products and trade
lessons.bigQuestion: How did a rainforest tree end up in your bicycle tyres?
objectives: To understand how products from the rainforest are traded around the world
successCriteria: All: name three products that come from rainforests
Most: describe how a product travels from forest to shop
Some: explain how trade can be fair to farmers
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness to the people who grow our food

keywords.def: something made or grown to sell
something useful that people can use
a stretchy material made from the sap of a tree
buying and selling between places
trade that pays farmers a fair price

hook.text: Look around your kitchen. Could anything have started its life in a rainforest?

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches fair trade. Allah says: give full measure and weigh with an even balance (al-Isra 17:35). The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was a trusted trader known for his honesty. Paying farmers fairly for rainforest products follows this teaching.

starter.q: Where do most rainforest animals live?

teach.heading: Products from the forest
teach.note: Rubber trees and cocoa trees first grew in South America. Today most cocoa is grown in West Africa.

teach.heading: Rubber
teach.note: Tapping does not kill the tree, so it can be used for many years: a sustainable use.

teach.heading: From forest to shop
teach.note: Trace cocoa beans from a farm in Ghana to a shop in the UK on the map.

teach.heading: Fair trade
bullets: Farmers should get a fair price
Some products carry a Fairtrade mark
Fairness is part of good trade
teach.note: Ask: who does the hardest work? Who gets the most money? Is that fair?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Rubber is made from latex, the white sap of the rubber tree.

practice.q: Put in order: ship, farm, shop, factory.
practice.model:
It starts where it grows: the farm.
Then it is made into the product: factory.
Then it travels: ship.
Last we buy it: shop.

practice.q: Name a product made from cocoa.
Why is tapping rubber trees a good way to use the forest?
practice.a: The trees stay alive and can be tapped for years

independent.q: Core: Make a flow chart showing how cocoa beans become a chocolate bar in a UK shop.
independent.a: Cocoa farm in West Africa, beans dried, factory makes chocolate, ship or lorry, UK shop

islamicLink.text: Allah says He made people successors (khulafa') on the earth (al-An'am 6:165), and that corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have done (ar-Rum 30:41). A Muslim is a steward: we may use the earth, but we must not waste or destroy it.

teach.heading: How we can care for it

exit.q: A steward:
